title: Evil is a lack (ST I.48–49)
hookLine: evil is not a thing, but the absence of a good that should be there

lines: DOES GOD HOLD EVIL IN BEING?
cards: A sweater comes out of the closet in the fall with a hole in the sleeve. You can point to the hole, push a finger through it. It's real enough to ruin the sweater.

But try to set the hole on the table by itself: there's nothing to pick up. The hole is only where wool should be and isn't. So, a hard question: if God holds every created thing in being, does he hold evil in being too?
Back near day three hundred, there was no quick answer. Thomas adds one piece: privation.

teach.b: Thomas starts from Genesis. In the Douay-Rheims: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good." If everything that has being is good, evil can't be one more thing on the list.

teach.h: EVIL: A GOOD THAT SHOULD BE THERE.
teach.b: So, following Augustine, Thomas says evil is a privation: the absence of a good that should be there. Not just any absence. A stone can't see, and nothing is wrong with the stone.
A person who has lost their sight is missing something a human eye is meant to have. Same lack of seeing; only one is a privation. Evil is always a lack measured against what a thing is for.
Then a second surprise: evil can only exist in something good.
A hole needs a sweater. Rot needs a tree. A lie needs a mind made for truth.
Even the worst cruelty is done by a real person, with real gifts, bent away from what those gifts are for. So there is no supreme evil, no dark rival to God.
A perfect evil would have to destroy every good, and so destroy itself. Now a warning. A lack is not unreal.
A missing kindness, a missing truth, a missing parent: these do terrible damage. Thomas isn't shrinking evil. He's saying it has no foothold of its own.
Paul makes the same shape practical, in Romans: "Be not overcome by evil, but overcome evil by good." You don't fight a hole by staring at it. You fill it.

how: Catholic teachers often explain evil, following Augustine and Thomas, as the absence of a good that ought to be present, and the idea comes up in homilies and classes on suffering and sin.

o: a dark power working against God's will
a punishment sent to correct a wrongdoer
the lack of a good that should be there

games.q: evil is a lack — tap the pairs.
p: a person who lost their sight
a good that should be there

s: for Thomas, evil is unreal, so it doesn't matter
a lack is real enough to do terrible damage. Thomas says evil has no being of its own, not that it's harmless.
Thomas says evil can only exist in something good
like a hole in a sweater: the lack needs a good subject to be a lack in.
Thomas teaches a supreme evil that rivals God
he says there's no supreme evil: a perfect evil would destroy every good, and itself with it.

games.q: you're Thomas. a student asks: if God made everything, and evil is real, didn't God make evil? what do you answer?
o: yes: God made evil along with everything else.
evil isn't a made thing; it's a good missing where it should be.
there's a supreme evil that made it, a rival to God.
games.why: Thomas, following Augustine, calls evil a privation: not a thing on the list of creation, but a lack in something good. and he rejects any supreme evil.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that feels wrong right now: a strained friendship, a habit you're ashamed of, a mess at work.
Ask Thomas's question of it, what good should be here and isn't, and name that good in a word or two: patience, honesty, rest.
If you pray, ask God for that one good by name; if not, notice that a missing good can be supplied, a little at a time.

wordCard.voice: Privation. The absence of a good that should be there. For Thomas, that is what evil is: not a thing God made, but a lack in something good. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: a lack, a being-deprived of something.

carryVoice: Your line: a hole, not a thing. Every hole sits in something good. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good.
Be not overcome by evil, but overcome evil by good.
